name: The Waukegan Industrial Shelf
description:
Waukegan was an industrial city before the word 'industrial' became a euphemism for 'expendable.' The lakefront that once hosted a naval training station and a pharmaceutical campus now hosts the northern terminus of GLMZ's automated cargo logistics network — a sprawl of container yards, drone maintenance hangars, and processing facilities where Lake Michigan's cargo platforms offload goods that will be distributed throughout the Corridor. The work that remains for human hands is the work machines can't do cheaply enough yet, which is a category that shrinks every fiscal quarter.

The old naval station — Great Lakes Naval Training Center, decommissioned by the remnant federal government in 2158 — was acquired by Ringo Defense Solutions in the sovereignty charter fire sale of 2161. Ringo converted it into a regional security operations base, which means the northern edge of Waukegan is a walled compound where private military contractors train, refit, and stage for operations throughout the upper GLMZ. The base employs 12,000 people and contributes exactly nothing to the surrounding community except a perimeter wall, a no-fly zone, and the occasional sound of live-fire exercises at 3 AM.

Between the cargo yards and the Ringo wall, the residential district survives the way organisms survive in extreme environments: by adapting to conditions that would kill anything designed for comfort. The housing stock is a mix of 20th-century bungalows — some of them literally a hundred and fifty years old, patched with whatever was available — and modular refugee housing units dropped by the GLMZ Metropolitan Authority during the Gulf Coast Displacement crisis of the 2070s. The modulars were supposed to be temporary. Temporary, in municipal planning, means 'until someone allocates a budget that will never be allocated.' They're still here. The people inside them have made them home, which is what people do.

The lakefront itself is poisoned. A century of industrial runoff, compounded by the cargo platform chemical discharge that nobody regulates because the platforms operate in federal — now corporate — waters, has made the shoreline a dead zone. The water is technically Lake Michigan. The color is not.

sights: Cargo platform drones descending in formation over the container yards, navigation lights blinking in synchronized patterns
The Ringo compound wall — three meters of reinforced concrete topped with sensor arrays, visible from most of the district
Modular housing units stacked two and three high, connected by improvised walkways and exterior staircases
The dead lakefront — grey-brown water, no vegetation, automated warning buoys marking chemical discharge zones
Old bungalow neighborhoods where century-old architecture meets salvaged solar panels and jury-rigged power taps
sounds: Container yard automation — the grinding of cargo cranes, the hiss of pneumatic seals, running 24 hours
Ringo live-fire exercises — distant but unmistakable, a sound the residents have learned to sleep through
Wind off the lake carrying a faint chemical whistle through gaps in the modular housing stacks
Children playing in the spaces between housing units, their games adapted to the narrow corridors available
The low thrum of the cargo maglev running containers south toward GLMZ's distribution centers
smells: Chemical lake — an acrid, metallic smell that residents stop noticing after a few months and visitors never forget
Diesel exhaust from the backup generators that keep the modular units running when the grid fails, which is often
Cooking smells from the housing corridors — a dense mix of Gulf Coast, Central American, and Southeast Asian cuisines, the smell of every displacement crisis blended together
Ozone and machine lubricant from the cargo yards
atmosphere.feel: A place that works hard and gets nothing for it. The cargo moves through Waukegan at enormous volume and none of it stops here. The wealth generated by the logistics network is measured in billions of Q and accrues to companies headquartered in buildings the residents of Waukegan will never enter. The community is real, the mutual aid is genuine, and the anger is justified. This is what a company town looks like when the company doesn't even bother to pretend it's a town.

demographics: Approximately 140,000 residents. Heavily working class, Tier 1-2. Significant Gulf Coast displacement population (roughly 30%). Large Latino community predating the displacement era. Ringo base personnel technically reside in Waukegan but exist in a separate jurisdiction and economy. Median age skews young — people leave when they can afford to, which means the ones who stay can't.
economy: Logistics labor — the cargo yards employ approximately 15,000 people in roles that automation hasn't eliminated yet. Ringo base support services. Informal economy is substantial: repair work, food service, unlicensed medical care. The nearest licensed medical facility is in The Threshold, twenty minutes south by Purple Line.
power_structure: No single authority. Ringo controls the northern perimeter. Axiom Logistics controls the cargo yards. The residential district falls into a jurisdiction gap — nominally under GLMZ Metropolitan Authority, which maintains a single administrative office staffed by two people who process complaints they cannot act on. Real authority is community-based: block captains, mutual aid networks, and the occasional intervention by whoever is currently running the local gray market.
dangers: Ringo perimeter enforcement — the compound's automated defense systems have a documented shoot-first protocol for the buffer zone
Cargo yard accidents — automation failures kill roughly twenty workers per year, classified as 'operational incidents'
Environmental exposure — the lakefront contamination causes elevated cancer rates that nobody is studying because nobody is funding the study
Jurisdiction void — no reliable law enforcement means disputes are settled by whatever means are available
Displacement violence — resource competition between established residents and newer refugee populations
opportunities: Cargo theft — the logistics network moves Q billions in goods through a district with no effective security
Ringo intelligence — the base leaks information through its support staff, who live in the community and talk
Mutual aid networks — the community infrastructure here is among the strongest in the upper Corridor
Labor organizing — the cargo yard workforce is large, angry, and increasingly coordinated
story_hooks: A cargo container from the Ringo base was accidentally routed to the civilian yard — and its contents don't match any known Ringo inventory
The lakefront contamination is getting worse, and a community health worker has data suggesting it's not just industrial runoff — someone is actively dumping
A Ringo contractor has gone AWOL into the residential district, carrying information worth enough to change jurisdictions

adjacent_to: Lake Michigan cargo platform array (east, water access)

frequented_by: Logistics workers — the cargo yard labor force that keeps GLMZ's supply chain moving
Ringo support personnel — contractors, maintenance workers, and service providers who live in the community
Displacement community organizers — people who turned refugee survival into permanent mutual aid infrastructure
Smugglers who exploit the gap between the cargo yard's enormous throughput and its imperfect inventory systems
